title: Littleton
name: Littleton
metaDescription: Littleton 1031 exchange guidance for historic downtown retail, Santa Fe corridor industrial, and Aspen Grove lifestyle center property south of Denver.

sections.html: Littleton is one of the older towns in the metro, sitting along the South Platte River south of Denver, and it kept a real historic downtown while the suburbs grew up around it. That downtown core, plus older industrial along Santa Fe Drive and newer retail near Aspen Grove, gives this submarket three distinct property types worth knowing apart.

sections.heading: Historic Downtown Runs on Small Buildings
sections.html:
Main Street in Littleton kept its early-1900s brick storefronts, and most of the retail down there sits in small, individually owned buildings rather than a single master-planned development. The Littleton-Downtown light rail station sits right at the edge of it, which has helped foot traffic stay steady even as bigger retail centers pulled shoppers elsewhere in the metro. A buyer looking at Main Street property should expect smaller floor plates and older mechanical systems, this stock predates modern retail construction by decades.

Littleton is also the county seat of Arapahoe County, and the Arapahoe County Justice Center sits just a few blocks from downtown. That courthouse presence supports a real cluster of legal and title-services office tenants near Main Street, a demand driver that has nothing to do with foot traffic or retail sales and is worth underwriting separately from the surrounding storefront leases.

sections.heading: What Actually Trades Here
sections.html:
Littleton's realistic property types break down as:

  • historic brick storefronts along Main Street and Alamo Avenue
  • light industrial and flex buildings along the Santa Fe Drive corridor
  • lifestyle center retail near Aspen Grove
  • small professional office buildings serving the local residential base

sections.heading: Santa Fe Drive Is a Different Asset Class
sections.html:
Older light industrial and flex buildings run along Santa Fe Drive and Highway 85, some dating back to Littleton's manufacturing and rail-era past. This stock trades on different fundamentals than the downtown retail, tenants here care about loading docks and clear height, not foot traffic, and a buyer should comp it against other south-metro industrial rather than against Main Street rents.

Aspen Grove, an open-air lifestyle center a few miles south of downtown, is a third distinct format, national retail and restaurant tenants in a newer outdoor mall layout. It leases more like a suburban shopping center than either the historic downtown or the industrial corridor.

The South Platte River corridor runs along Littleton's eastern edge and carries its own flood plain mapping that a buyer needs to check on any parcel close to the river, industrial or otherwise. A property sitting inside a mapped flood zone can face insurance costs and lender requirements that a similar building two blocks further from the river wouldn't carry.

sections.heading: Diligence Points for Littleton Property
sections.html: On downtown buildings, get a mechanical and structural review given the age of the stock, and confirm any historic district design review requirements before assuming a renovation timeline. On Santa Fe corridor industrial, check environmental history given the area's manufacturing past, a phase one assessment is worth the cost here more than in most south-metro submarkets. On downtown storefronts, confirm any recorded party-wall agreement between adjacent buildings, a common feature on narrow lots built before modern platting standards, since it can affect what a new owner is allowed to do with an exterior wall shared with the building next door.

sections.heading: Positioning a Littleton Identification
sections.html: A downtown Littleton storefront pairs naturally with a Highlands Ranch or Centennial property to balance a small historic retail asset against a larger, newer commercial building elsewhere in the south Denver metro. Santa Fe corridor industrial is often identified alongside Denver Tech Center office for a mix of asset classes rather than concentrating an exchange in a single property type. A qualified intermediary should confirm which taxing jurisdiction applies on any Littleton parcel that sits close to the Arapahoe and Douglas county line, since a handful of properties on the city's southern edge cross that boundary. A rent roll comparison across Littleton's three property types, downtown storefront, Santa Fe industrial, and Aspen Grove retail, should never be run as a single blended average, since each type responds to a different tenant base and a different set of demand drivers. A replacement property identification for Littleton should note the exact corridor by name in the paperwork, rather than only the city, since a downtown storefront and a Santa Fe corridor warehouse have almost nothing in common as underwriting exercises.

faqs.q: Is historic downtown Littleton retail a good 1031 replacement property?
faqs.a: It can be, but expect smaller floor plates and older mechanical systems given the age of the buildings. Get a structural and mechanical review before underwriting a renovation budget.

faqs.q: What kind of environmental diligence does Santa Fe corridor industrial need?
faqs.a: A phase one environmental assessment is worth doing here given the corridor's manufacturing and rail-era history, more so than in most other south-metro submarkets.

faqs.q: How is Aspen Grove different from downtown Littleton retail?
faqs.a: It's a newer open-air lifestyle center with national retail and restaurant tenants, leasing more like a suburban shopping center than the small individually owned storefronts downtown.

faqs.q: Does the Littleton-Downtown light rail station help retail foot traffic?
faqs.a: Yes, it has helped keep foot traffic steady on Main Street even as larger retail centers elsewhere in the metro pulled shoppers away.

faqs.q: What does a Littleton identification typically pair with?
faqs.a: A downtown storefront often pairs with a Highlands Ranch or Centennial property for size balance, while Santa Fe corridor industrial is often paired with Denver Tech Center office for asset-class diversification.
